# Preface
---

> Among the Adityas, I am Vishnu; among the luminaries, I am the radiant Sun.
> Among the Maruts, I am Marichi; among the stars, I am the Moon.
<note>original: "आदित्यानामहंविष्णुर्ज्योतिषांरविरंशुमान् ॥ मरीचिर्मरुतामस्मि नक्षत्राणामहंशशी ।"</note>
-> — Bhagavad Gita <-

The Sun, Moon, Earth, stars, and other celestial spheres, manifested from the divine brilliance of the Ruler of the Universe, have been established as the causes of the joys and sorrows of all living beings. This reality was demonstrated to future generations by divine sages like Narada through texts on Astrology, Kerala <note>A system of astrology from Southern India</note>, Panchapakshi <note>The "Five Birds" system of divination</note>, Svarashastra <note>The science of breath and sound</note>, Palmistry, and Ramal <note>Geomancy or divination by dots and lines</note>. Consequently, great scholars such as Bhaskaracharya, Jagam, Adam, Daniel, Luqman the Wise, Yavanacharya, Napoleon Bonaparte, and others, wrote numerous books in Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, Urdu, and English according to their intellectual prowess. This book, titled "**Ramal Shastra or Ionian Predictive Astrology**," is the essence of all those works written for the benefit of the unlearned.

Because this science of Ramal was once famous everywhere among the Yavana <note>Historically referring to Greeks or Ionians, and later to Persians and Arabs</note> people, a courageous scholar from this land of Aryavarta <note>The ancient name for Northern India</note> traveled to those countries and learned this extraordinary and rare science in their script. While preserving the original terms and certain methods from the Yavana language, he disseminated the texts in the Sanskrit language. No one should forget the name of that Yavanacharya.

By the will of God, as the opportunity has arisen to reprint this second edition, many improvements have been made. Notes, examples, and additional information have been provided in various places to resolve doubts, making this edition one and a half times larger than the first. As before, it is divided into three parts. The first part (pages 1 to 94) covers the origin of this science, the use of dice, <term>Mantra-siddhi</term> <note>The mastery or empowerment of sacred chants</note>, the methods for preparing a birth chart, the influence of the Sun, Moon, and other planets, the zodiac signs and the <insert>five</insert> elements, the friendships and enmities of the elements, the descriptions of the qualities of the <term>Shakals</term> <note>The sixteen geomantic figures or "shapes" used in Ramal</note>, the determination of auspicious days, and the tools and numbers required for answering queries.

<summary>This preface introduces a manual on Ramal Shastra (geomancy), tracing its lineage from divine sages to historical figures like Napoleon, and explaining its translation from Yavana (Ionian/Persian) sources into Sanskrit and Marathi.</summary>
<keywords>Ramal Shastra, Astrology, Yavanacharya, Geomancy, Divination, Aryavarta, Elements, Shakals</keywords>

The decisions and various other matters are contained in the second part, from pages 95 to 198, which includes a complete collection of questions. Each question is accompanied by easy methods for resolution based on the foundations of all relevant texts. In the third part, from pages 199 to 216, the book concludes with reflections on the outcomes occurring in the year, the month, and each day, as well as events affecting the country.

Readers should not attempt to provide predictions from the collection of questions in the second and third parts without first gaining complete information and study of the first part. Once the study is complete, one should provide answers after considering the circumstances of time and place <note>original: "desh-kaal-sthiti," a traditional concept emphasizing that predictions must be adapted to the specific context of the person and era</note> and reflecting on the instructions given periodically throughout the text. Readers should prepare the necessary dice <note>original: "phanse," used in divination systems like Ramala</note> required for their practice.

This book is not a work of pure literature; because its composition is based on original words from Persian, Urdu, and other languages, there is a lack of formal grammar and prosody <note>the study of poetic meters</note>, which occasionally leads to distortions in meaning. Therefore, readers are requested to focus on the original intent and act according to the <term>logic of the swan and the milk</term> <note>original: "Neer-Ksheer Nyaya." In Indian mythology, a swan is said to be able to separate milk from water; this term asks the reader to extract the essence of the truth while discarding any linguistic flaws.</note>.

->— The Publisher.<-

# Ramala Shastra.
<note>Ramala Shastra is a form of divination or geomancy, originally influenced by Arabic traditions (Raml) and integrated into Indian astrological practices.</note>

->* * * * *<-

->To the one whose form is infinite consciousness, unconditioned by direction, time, or space;<-
->whose essence is self-realization alone; salutations to that peaceful radiance. Auspiciousness!<-
->A desire for the company of the virtuous; an appreciation for the merits of others; humility before the teacher;<-
->a passion for learning; devotion to one's own spouse; a fear of public scandal;<-
->devotion to the Lord <note>original: "Shulini" - the spear-bearer, referring to Shiva</note>; the power of self-restraint; and freedom from the company of the wicked;<-
->salutations to those noble men in whom these pure qualities reside. || 1 ||<-

**Meaning:** I bow to those superior men—verily to the Divine <note>original: "Narayana"</note>—who are adorned with all these pure qualities: the desire for the company of the good, love for the excellent virtues of others, humility toward the Guru, the diligent pursuit of knowledge, devotion to one's own wife, fear of ill-repute, incomparable devotion to the Lord of the Universe, the strength to control oneself, and the wish to avoid the company of the wicked.

## The Origin of Ramala Shastra.

->On the beautiful peak of Kailas, adorned with various trees and vines,<-
->shining like pure crystal, filled with the songs of various birds,<-
->surrounded by many peaks and decorated with gems and lapis lazuli,<-
->Gauri <note>The goddess Parvati</note>, with a heart full of love, spoke to the Lord of the Mountain <note>Shiva</note>. || 2 ||<-

**Meaning:** Seeing the Lord Mahadeva <note>Shiva</note> seated in great bliss upon a throne encrusted with jewels, lapis lazuli, and topazes, in the center of the crystal-bright peaks of Kailas—where various trees and vines flourish, the sounds of diverse birds echo everywhere, and mountain peaks rise in every direction—Parvati addressed him:

->|| O Lord, God of Gods, whose forehead is adorned by the moon ||<-
->|| Tell me the supreme knowledge arising from questions of good and evil ||<-
->|| Of the past, the future, and likewise the present ||<-
->|| The science of all times, by which the seeker may know || 3 ||<-

**Meaning:** O God of Gods, appearing in a peaceful form and wearing the moon upon your matted hair! Please, out of your grace, tell me the easy method by which seekers may understand the state of things occurring in the present, past, and future at all times! <note>The speaker here is the goddess Parvati, addressing Lord Shiva.</note>

->|| Hearing the words of Parvati, Shiva’s mind was filled with joy ||<-
->|| In that moment, a drop of nectar fell from the moon before him ||<-
->|| That drop of supreme nectar was four-sided and four-cornered ||<-
->|| As soon as the drop fell, the elements like fire arrived || 4 ||<-

**Meaning:** Upon hearing Parvati’s request, Mahadeva <note>A name for Shiva meaning 'Great God'</note> became absorbed in extreme bliss and began to sway. With that swaying, a drop of nectar <note>original: "sudha-bindu"</note> fell down from the moon on his head in a quadrangular shape, and from it, the elements of light (fire), air, and others were produced.

->|| In the four directions of that drop were Fire, Air, Water, and Earth ||<-
->|| Fire and Water in the East; Air in the South; Earth and Water in the North ||<-
->|| Between us both, this science was produced through divine play ||<-
->|| Therefore, it shall be known by the name of 'Ramal' on the surface of the earth || 5 ||<-

**Meaning:** Because that drop turned toward the East, West, North, and South directions in sequence, the lords of the four directions—Fire, Air, Water, and Earth—came in order and took a taste of their respective portions. Seeing this, Mahadeva, in order to establish the structure of this creation according to his own Universal Form <term>Virat Deha: the macrocosmic body of the universe</term>, imagined that drop to be the Universal Form itself. As those directional guardians tasted it, he established the elements accordingly. In that Universal Form, the head is the East governed by Fire; from the mouth to the heart is the West governed by Air; from the stomach to the ankles is the North governed by Water; and from the ankles to the soles of the feet is the South governed by Earth. These elements...

Having established them in their respective places, and because the elements of Fire, Air, and Water are light in weight while the Earth element is heavy, He combined all these elements with one another. He then assigned the <term>Devatas and Upadevatas</term><note>Primary and secondary deities or celestial governing forces</note> to these elements. The deities were established as follows: for the **Fire** element—Jupiter, Rahu, the Sun, and Ketu; for the **Air** element—Venus, Mars, Mercury, and a portion of Venus; for the **Water** element—Jupiter, Mars, a portion of the Moon, and the Moon; and for the **Earth** element—Mercury, Saturn, and portions of the Sun and Saturn. After establishing these deities in the form of the nine planets (<term>Navagrahas</term>) upon the <term>Virat Deha</term><note>The "Universal Body" or Macrocosm, representing the universe as a single living entity</note>, He divided this Universal Form into twelve parts and established the Zodiac signs (<term>Rashis</term>). Giving these signs a fixed form upon the body, He assigned them thus: **Aries** on the head; **Taurus** on the face; **Gemini** from the throat to the heart; **Cancer** on the heart; **Leo** on the stomach; **Virgo** on the waist; **Libra** on the navel; **Scorpio** on the genitals; **Sagittarius** on the thighs; **Capricorn** on the knees; **Aquarius** on the ankles; and **Pisces** on the soles of the feet. Having divided them in this manner, He further divided them into 16 parts (fragments), gave those parts names and forms, and through them, wrote the science of knowing the past, present, and future, which He then taught to Parvati; and:

> Just as the moon, when lacking its digits <note>original: "kalahinashchandrama"</note>, does not shine in a mirror;
> So too is the body devoid of nectar, and from that comes the human form.
> When a forest is to be doubled, then one surely becomes constant.
> This is filled with points <note>dots/bindus</note> and by numbers such as eight.
> From these, others measured by the mind become like children.
> Neither more nor less are born than these sixteen marked forms. || 6 ||

**Meaning:—** First, the point (<note>original: "bindu"</note> $\circ$) that fell from the head of Lord Shiva was without digits <note>phases of light</note>. Its four divisions

By the union of points, four such lines ☰ were formed; this became the Full Moon <note>Prakriti or Nature</note>. [The Greeks <note>original: "Yavan", referring here to practitioners of Greco-Arabic geomancy</note> call this 'Jama'at' <note>Arabic for 'gathering' or 'community'</note>]. Since the origin of all stationary and moving things results from the relationship between Nature (the Mother) and the Spirit (the Father), the point (•) which remains in its state is the Spirit <note>Purush</note>, and the growth (-) resulting from the union of two points is Nature <note>Prakriti</note>. With the help of these four lines ☰ and these four points ⁞, sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons were produced—meaning the two became four, the four became eight, and the eight became sixteen—thus completing the sixteen phases <note>Shodash Kala</note>. Because the path of their creation ended at sixteen, the Greeks gave these sixteen signs the name 'Shakal' <note>Arabic: 'Shakl', meaning form or sign</note> in their language.

### Names Given by Lord Shiva

> || The eloquent one, the hot-rayed one, the fallen one, the wise one, the messenger ||
> || The crooked one, the son of Saturn, the slow-mover, the sharp-rayed one, the teacher of demons ||
> || The learned one, the wanderer, the poet, the twin, the cool-rayed one, and the gentle one ||
> || With the letters A, Va, Da, Ha in sequence, the wise play with these planets || 7 ||
<note>original: "Vagmi lohita ushnaguviduratha..." This Sanskrit verse lists the poetic names of the sixteen geomantic signs associated with planetary influences.</note>

**Meaning:**—Names were given to those sixteen signs <note>Shakals</note>: 1. Vagmi (The Eloquent), 2. Tikshnanshu (The Sharp-rayed), 3. Pata (The Fallen), 4. Saumya (The Gentle), 5. Daityarchi (The Teacher of Demons), 6. Mandaga (The Slow-mover), 7. Sauri (The Son of Saturn), 8. Lohita (The Red One), 9. Vidhu (The Moon), 10. Ushnagu (The Hot-rayed), 11. Suri (The Wise), 12. Vakra (The Crooked), 13. Ara (The Messenger), 14. Kavi (The Poet), 15. Bodhana (The Awakener), and 16. Shitanshu (The Cool-rayed). By writing the numerical sequence A. Va. Da. Ha. <note>A system for assigning numerical values to letters</note>, the method for wise men to use these planets was described.

> || These are known as bound to the planets and the rising signs ||

**Meaning:**—In this mathematical science joined with the planets, the twelve zodiac signs and planets were bound together in a long circular form ॰॰ ⁝ ⁝ ⁝ ⁝ ॰॰. **Meaning:**—The results of the questions were written on birch bark <note>Bhurjapatra</note>, and after blessing the text, it was hidden away in a cave of Mount Kailash.

# Time Revealed in the Mortal World.

> || At the end of the Dvapara Age, the eminent sage Adam ||
> || Performed great penance, shining like a second Sun || 10 ||
<note>original: "युगेच द्वापरस्यांते आदमो मुनिपुंगवः..." The text identifies the biblical/Islamic Adam as a Vedic-style Rishi (sage) appearing at the end of the Dvapara Yuga, the third age in Hindu cosmology.</note>

Meaning: — The sage 'Adam', who shines in this world and the next through the power of his penance like the sun, brought this book to fame in the mortal world at the end of the Dvapara Age.

## Metals for the Dice.

Copper (for the Sun), Silver (for the Moon), Brass (for Mars), Lead (for Mercury), Gold (for Jupiter), Tin (for Venus), and Iron (for Saturn); among the nine planets, Rahu and Ketu <note>The North and South Lunar Nodes</note> do not represent measures of time, and since these planets give results similar to Saturn, it is not mentioned anywhere in the Ionian <note>term: Yavan (Greek/Persian/Islamic)</note> or Sanskrit texts to use metals for those planets. One should take 3 *masas* <note>A traditional unit of weight, roughly 1 gram</note> of each of these seven metals, totaling 21 *masas*. Carefully observe the method shown below for making eight pieces from these metals.

## Method of Preparing the Dice.

> || In the science of Ramal, the dice are primary; I shall state their rule ||
> || Mark four dots above, and two dots below ||
> || Mark one dot on the side; thus make eight firm dice ||
> || They are said to be joined by a central pin, four in number || 11 ||
<note>term: Ramal (Geomancy). This refers to a divination system using dots and lines, often associated with Middle Eastern origins but integrated here into Indian practice.</note>

Meaning: — Taking the metals of the six planets mentioned above and melting them, <insert> make one long four-sided strip and cut it into eight </insert> pieces such that all four sides are equal. On the upper part of each piece, make four clear dot marks like this ः ः and on the bottom part of that four-sided piece, make two dot marks like ः. When that piece is held between the index finger and the thumb, the side facing you—

Once the dot markings **° °** have been placed on the visible side and the back in this manner, drill a hole straight through the center of the two remaining open sides of the piece, large enough for a rod to pass through. In the same way, prepare the markings and holes on the remaining seven pieces. Then, take two iron rods and slide four pieces onto each rod. ### The Auspicious Time for Making the Dice.

> "In this way, one should create the pair of dice-strings when the Sun enters Aries. One should then mark the zeros <note>original: 'shunya' or dots</note> on the dice. On the day of the Aries Transit, one should begin using them for divination. On an auspicious day, the wise practitioner should cast them upon the board to seek answers." (Verse 12)

**Meaning:** As described above, two strings of four pieces each should be prepared on the day of the Tropical Aries Transit <note>original: 'Sayana Mesha' - this occurs annually around March 20th or 21st when the Sun enters the sign of Aries</note>. The zeros should be marked on the pieces that same day. To see the results of a query, the dice should be cast upon a board on an auspicious day.

### Preparing the Board.

> "One should construct a smooth wooden seat <note>a platform or board</note> two and a quarter cubits <note>original: 'sapada-dvi-hasta'</note> long and half that in width. Upon it, one should spread sand brought from the banks of the Ganges or from pure earth, collected by a twelve-year-old boy and free from insects." (Verse 13)

<term>Dice (Phanse)</term> — Rectangular blocks used for divination, often strung together.
<term>Tropical Aries (Sayana Mesha)</term> — The Spring Equinox, considered a powerful time for beginning spiritual or technical works.
<term>Aries Transit (Mesha Sankranti)</term> — The moment the sun enters the constellation of Aries.
<term>Board (Pattika)</term> — The prepared surface used for casting the dice.
<term>Rod (Salai)</term> — The metal axis on which the dice rotate.
<term>Two and a quarter cubits (Sapadadvi-hasta)</term> — A traditional measurement; a 'hasta' is roughly the length of a forearm (18 inches).

Meaning: Prepare a board made of sandalwood or another oily wood, measuring 54 <term>angulas</term> <note>a traditional unit of measurement approximately equal to the width of a finger</note> in length and 30 <term>angulas</term> in width. Have a twelve-year-old boy bring clean sand from the banks of the Ganges or from another purified piece of ground. Spread this sand upon the board and draw the <term>kundali</term> <note>a square or circular chart used to map geomantic figures</note> using the stylus described below.

### Preparing the Stylus

-> The stylus in the hand of one skilled in Ramal should have a long nib; <-
-> Its entire body should be free of knots or joints. <-
-> Likewise, the two halves of its nib should be equal and symmetrical; <-
-> O Destroyer of Tripura <note>an invocation of the God Shiva</note>, only then is the material world truly revealed. (Verse 14) <-
<note>original: "रमलनिपुणहस्ते लेखणी लंबचंचू..." - This Sanskrit verse outlines the aesthetic and functional requirements for the divination tool.</note>

Meaning: For the practice of <term>Ramal</term> <note>the art of geomancy, or divination by earth and signs</note>, one should use a stylus that is long, smooth (without knots), and has a tip that is long and evenly split.

### Attaining Mastery of the Mantra

-> Om Hrim, to the ever-auspicious Samba-Shiva, to the Innocent Bhairava, Om Hum Phat Svaha! <-
<note>original: "ॐ ह्रीं सांब सदाशिवाय भोलाभैरवाय ॐ हूँ फट् स्वाह:" - A tantric invocation to the deity Shiva in his fierce and gentle forms.</note>

This mantra should be mastered by chanting it 500,000 times in a secluded place or in a cremation ground.

### Times for Consulting the Oracle and Reasons for Refusal

On Tuesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays; on the 3rd, 5th, 13th, 16th, 21st, 24th, and 25th dates of the Islamic calendar; if the sky is unseasonably overcast; during the period of 11.5 <term>ghatikas</term> <note>a ghatika is 24 minutes; 11.5 ghatikas is approximately 4 hours and 36 minutes</note> after sunrise or after 11.5 <term>ghatikas</term> of the night have passed; and if in the 1st or 15th house of the question <term>kundali</term> either of these two <term>shakals</term> <note>geomantic figures or signs</note> <unclear>≡</unclear> <unclear>⁝⁝</unclear> appear; or if the petitioner is not physically present before the astrologer. Furthermore, in the <term>Hora Chart</term> <note>a table of planetary hours</note> provided hereafter, the letters Sh., M., and A. are placed to the right of the <term>shakals</term> under each day: 'Sh' denotes an Auspicious time, 'M' denotes a Middling time, and 'A' denotes an Inauspicious time.

Where the letter 'A' appears among the initial letters of the words, in the first column to the left, the <term>Ghatikas</term> <note>A traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> and hours provided from sunrise to sunset and sunset to sunrise indicate inauspicious times. During these specific times, or if the astrologer himself is caught in physical or mental distress, one should not prepare a <term>Kundali</term> <note>A birth chart or horary figure</note> or provide predictions regarding the name of a thief, buried treasure, or <term>Mushti-Prashna</term> <note>A 'fist-question' where the astrologer divines what object is hidden in the querent's hand</note>. As this has been stated in both Sanskrit and <term>Yavana</term> <note>Literally 'Greek' or 'Ionian,' referring here to Perso-Arabic or Western astrological traditions</note> texts, astrologers must necessarily pay attention to it. One should examine questions only after excluding the aforementioned reasons and times.

**Example:** On Sunday morning, at the influence of 7.5 <term>Ghatikas</term>—meaning around 9 o'clock—if a querent arrives and begins to ask a question, the astrologer should look under the 'Sunday' heading in the following <term>Hora</term> <note>Hourly planetary influence</note> table. Looking ahead of the 3rd hour or 7.5 <term>Ghatikas</term>, the <term>Shakals</term> <note>Geomantic figures or symbols</note> $\equiv$ and <term>$\overset{\circ}{O}$</term> are present. Since the letter 'M' <note>Standing for 'Madhyam' or mediocre/average</note> is in front of them, it is a mediocre time. However, it is prescribed that if the figure $\equiv$ appears in the first house of the chart, one should not give a prediction, because that same figure, acting as the <term>Hora</term>, is considered the 'rising' or the <term>Lagna</term> <note>The Ascendant or first house</note>. Yet, when considering the time, since the <term>Hora</term> of these two figures $\equiv$ and <term>$\overset{\circ}{O}$</term> lasts for one period of 2.5 <term>Ghatikas</term> (or 1 hour), the first figure belongs to the first 1.25 <term>Ghatikas</term> and the second to the next 1.25. If the astrologer practices even finer discernment, the <term>Tattva</term> <note>The elemental essence or 'vibration' of that specific moment</note> of that time will also come to his mind. Anyway, since the querent arrived at 9 o'clock—during the 3rd hour—the figure <term>$\overset{\circ}{O}$</term> was in effect at that time, so there is no harm in examining the question. Because knowledge of <term>Ghatikas</term> and such has recently been disappearing among astrologers, this <term>Hora</term> table will be quite useful if a watch/clock is used.

## Method of Casting Dice for Inquiries.

> <note>original Sanskrit: ॥ लह्यानं पाशके योज्यं स्वेष्टदेवं गुरुन्स्मरन् ॥ ॥ पाशकं मंत्रयेदादौ सप्तवारं ततः क्षिपेत् ॥ १५ ॥</note>
> "One should arrange the Lahyana figure on the dice while remembering one's chosen deity and Guru. First, consecrate the dice with the mantra seven times, and then cast them." (Verse 15)

Meaning:—The astrologer should take the dice in the right palm and keep these four signs <insert>

# Method for Preparing the Chart

> <note>original: "पाशको च ततो योज्यौ प्रस्तारं कारयेत्सुधीः ॥ वक्ष्यमाण प्रकारेण तस्मात्प्रश्नं वदेद्बुधः ॥ १६ ॥"</note>
> *The wise one should cast the dice and then create the spread; following the method to be described, the learned practitioner should then declare the answer to the query.* — 16

Meaning: To provide an answer to a query, one must cast the dice and prepare the chart as follows:

In the figure shown to the side, numbers have been placed first so that the student understands the positions; these are the primary houses following the sequence of the omens. In this sequence, the 1st position contains the first small <term>shakl</term> <note>shakl: a geomantic figure or sign</note> (Tariq $\frac{\circ}{..}$); the 2nd position contains the second <term>shakl</term> (Kabzul Dakhil $\frac{॥}{\circ}$); the 3rd position contains the third <term>shakl</term> (Kabzul Kharij $\frac{\circ}{॥}$); and so on. One should understand that these 16 <term>shakls</term> are considered fixed in those specific positions as a reference. Because these fixed signs never change their base positions, this is called the "Omen Sequence." However, at the time of an actual query, one must interpret the results based only on the specific <term>shakls</term> that are formed according to the seeker's timing as soon as the dice are cast. To ensure the student does not encounter obstacles while interpreting the results, they must draw this "House Chart" before casting the query. Regarding the method of drawing the chart, students should follow the description in <term>Yavana Shastra</term> <note>Yavana Shastra: Literally "Greek/Foreign Science," referring here to the Indo-Persian tradition of Ramal astrology</note> which dictates drawing from right to left.

## Names of the Chart Divisions

The positions 1, 2, 3, and 4 in the chart are named <term>Ummahat</term> <note>Arabic: "Mothers"</note>; positions 5, 6, 7, and 8 are named <term>Binat</term> <note>Arabic: "Daughters"</note>; positions 9, 10, 11, and 12 are named <term>Mutawallidat</term> <note>Arabic: "Progeny/Born ones"</note>; and positions 13, 14, 15, and 16 are named <term>Zawaidat</term> or <term>Zaidat</term> <note>Arabic: "Appendices/Extra ones"</note>. These names apply both to the numbers in the base House Chart and to the specific <term>shakls</term> that fall into those positions during a seeker's query. For example: "the signs in the <term>Binat</term>" should be understood as the signs that appeared there during the casting of the query. And the original signs in the <term>Binat</term>...

With this, the complete chart is prepared.

### The Method of Multiplying Figures

Multiplying two dots (0, 0) results in a line (-). Multiplying two lines (-, -) also results in a single line (-). However, multiplying a dot and a line (0, -) results in a dot (0). In short, the product of two <term>dissimilar</term><note>original: 'vishama'</note> signs is a dot (0), and the product of two <term>similar</term><note>original: 'sama'</note> signs (whether they be dots or lines) is a line (-). Readers should keep this rule well in mind. Since all subsequent steps involve multiplication, if a dot is placed where a line should be, or a line where a dot should be due to an oversight, the entire chart will be false and the predictions will be contrary to reality. Even when exercising caution, it is necessary to check if a mistake has occurred; therefore, the following "rule of thumb" method should be noted.

To prepare the figure for the 9th position, take the figures from positions 2 and 1: $\begin{smallmatrix} \circ \\ \circ \\ \circ \\ \circ \end{smallmatrix}$ and $\begin{smallmatrix} = \\ = \\ = \\ = \end{smallmatrix}$. Upon multiplying them according to the rule stated above, the figure $\begin{smallmatrix} \circ \\ \circ \\ = \\ \circ \end{smallmatrix}$ is formed; place this in the 9th position. Then, taking the figures from positions 4 and 3: $\begin{smallmatrix} \circ \\ - \\ - \\ \circ \end{smallmatrix}$ and $\begin{smallmatrix} \circ \\ \circ \\ = \\ \circ \end{smallmatrix}$, their multiplication results in $\begin{smallmatrix} = \\ \circ \\ = \\ \circ \end{smallmatrix}$, which is established in the 10th position.

<note>The author uses '=' and '-' interchangeably for lines in the diagrams. In Ramala (Persian-derived geomancy), the logic follows binary addition: Even + Even = Even; Odd + Odd = Even; Even + Odd = Odd.</note>

**Group of questions for the 1st House and Figure: (The House of Body)**
Description of the entire body, God, facial features, lifespan, birthplace, considerations of happiness and sorrow, health, death, success and failure, profit and loss, the beginning of an undertaking, high or low status, sin and merit, strength and weakness, honor and insult, buying and selling, life, peace, remedies, long-distance travel of children, friends of brothers, brothers of friends, a boat (ship) that has gone far into the water, considerations of caste, subtle matters, politics, the King's father, and the petitioner's mental anxieties, etc. This is a small figure and represents the face of the <term>Virat Purusha</term><note>The Universal Man or Supreme Being in Vedic cosmology.</note>; the petitioner themselves is also connected to this house.

**Group of questions for the 2nd House and Figure: (The House of Wealth)**
Considerations of acquiring wealth, poverty, worldly happiness, helpers, self-help, profit in trade, movable property, buying and selling, richness and poverty, religiousness, stinginess, joy and sorrow, administering medicine, brothers of secret enemies, fathers of friends, the reputation and trade of children; if it is a man's chart, considerations of his wife's death, and if it is a woman's chart, considerations of her husband's death; partners and the death of enemies, shares, growth of property, money given as a loan, the condition of a patient and their food, the condition of small infants, profit and loss of a fixed matter, the arrangement of marriage ceremonies, legal practice, lawyers, eating and drinking, workers, enmity, considerations of women, and enmity with low-minded people.

### Further Considerations

The group of questions for the 13th house and its figure: The seeker's appearance, qualities, news, thoughts on the <term>enemy's</term> wealth, etc. This house maintains a relationship with houses 1, 5, and 9. Its figure is <term>Naki</term> <gloss>$\begin{smallmatrix} \circ \\ \text{I} \\ \circ \\ \circ \end{smallmatrix}$</gloss>.

The group of questions for the 14th house and its figure: Considerations of truth and falsehood, the nature of the task, success or failure, sexual union, etc. This house maintains a relationship with houses 2, 6, and 10. Its figure will show <term>Utapatul</term> <gloss>$\begin{smallmatrix} \circ \\ \circ \\ \circ \\ \text{I} \end{smallmatrix}$</gloss>.

The group of questions for the 15th house and its figure: The seeker's mental state, thoughts on the jury <note>panchas</note> and the mediator. This house maintains a relationship with houses 3, 7, and 11. The <term>Ramala experts</term> <note>practitioners of Ramala Shastra, a Persian-influenced system of divination using dots and lines</note> call this the <term>Channasthan</term> <note>hidden or secret house</note>. Its figure is <term>Ijjatma</term> <gloss>$\begin{smallmatrix} \text{I} \\ \circ \\ \circ \\ \text{I} \end{smallmatrix}$</gloss>.

The group of questions for the 16th house and its figure: Mental disposition, future success in tasks, peace, loss, etc. This house maintains a relationship with houses 4, 8, and 12. Its figure is <term>Tarikh</term> <gloss>$\begin{smallmatrix} \circ \\ \circ \\ \circ \\ \circ \end{smallmatrix}$</gloss>.

According to the method previously described for creating the <term>Kundali</term> <note>horoscope or birth chart</note>, once the chart is prepared, one half—consisting of houses 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 13, and 15—is beneficial to the seeker's interests. The other half—consisting of houses 5, 6, 7, 8, 11, 12, 14, and 16—is contrary to the seeker's desires. The seeker should deliberate after observing the auspicious and inauspicious houses and the figures within them in both these parts.

Some <term>astrologers</term>, no matter how many wives, children, or brothers and sisters a seeker has, provide readings for all of them based only on the 7th, 5th, and 3rd houses respectively. Because of this, the predictions often fail.

### The Refinement of the Elements

->|| The Sages have fashioned the science of Ramal based on the four elements ||<-
->|| Their variations are exactly sixteen; they neither increase nor decrease ||<-
->|| Therefore, in Ramal, sixteen figures were created ||<-
->|| And the wise have likewise fixed sixteen positions in the spread || 19 ||<-

**Meaning:** Fire, Air, Water, and Earth—these four elements alone are considered the fundamental causes of this science of Ramal <term>Ramal Shastra: The art of geomancy, originally of Arabic origin (Raml), adapted into Sanskrit and Marathi traditions</term>. Since each element possesses four sub-variations, the elemental refinement <note>Tattva-Samskara</note> performed on the 16 figures <term>Shakal: The geomantic figures or signs</term> is written as follows:

**Fire Element:** Youthful stage, yellow complexion, tall, proportionate body, wise, prone to anger, joyful, capable of completing tasks fully, masculine in form, and ruler of the East. The four figures of this Fire element are: <gloss>$\overset{\circ \circ}{\circ}$</gloss> <gloss>$\overset{\text{I}}{\circ}$</gloss> <gloss>$\overset{\circ \circ}{\circ}$</gloss> <gloss>$\overset{\text{I}}{\circ}$</gloss> <note>These represent specific geomantic signs like Albus or Puer, categorized here by their fiery nature</note>.

**Air Element:** Young adult stage, red complexion, tall and somewhat stout, restless yet peaceful, talkative, moderately successful in tasks, masculine in form, and ruler of the West. The four figures of this Air element are: <gloss>$\overset{\circ}{\circ \circ}$</gloss> <gloss>$\overset{\text{I}}{\circ \circ}$</gloss> <gloss>$\overset{\circ}{\circ \circ}$</gloss> <gloss>$\overset{\text{I}}{\circ \circ}$</gloss>.

**The Water Element:** <note>Marathi: Jalatattva</note> Represents adulthood, a fair complexion (exceedingly beautiful), and medium height. The temperament is neither fickle nor angry. It is feminine in form and occasionally presents obstacles to the completion of tasks. It rules the North direction. The four geomantic figures <note>shakls</note> associated with the Water element are: 〓/○, ○/〓, ○/○, and ○/○.

**The Earth Element:** <note>Marathi: Prithvitattva</note> Represents old age, a dark complexion, and a somewhat stout body. It is associated with a wicked intellect; it is destructive to tasks, appearing sweet on the outside but harboring bitterness within. It is feminine in form. This element tends to stand alone. Even if it happens to interact with other elements, it always prioritizes its own qualities; for this reason, the Lord who moves the world did not keep this element close to Himself. It rules the South direction. The four geomantic figures associated with the Earth element are: 〓/○, ≡/।, ○/≡, and ≡/○.

## The Characteristics of the Figures <note>original: Shaklancha Sanskar; refers to the inherent nature or 'purification' of the geomantic signs</note>

1. $\substack{\circ \\ \equiv}$ The name of this figure is *Lahyan* <note>Laetitia</note>—it is of the Brahmin <note>The priestly or scholarly social class</note> caste, fair-complexioned, and fond of eating sweet food. <page-num>30</page-num>

2. $\frac{\circ}{\circ}$ This is named **Kabzatul Dakhil** <note>Arabic: *Qabd al-Dakhil*, meaning "Inward Gain" or "Taking In"</note>:—Of the Warrior caste <term>Kshatriya</term>, reddish complexion, sweet-spoken, black eyes with red streaks, knowledgeable in the arts of architecture and craftsmanship <term>Shilpashastra</term>, young, of medium height, long hair, round face, elongated neck. Resides in temples, shops, or on the pathways. It is respected, wears fine garments, eats sweet foods, and collects pearls, rubies, and gold.

3. $\frac{\circ}{\circ}$ This is named **Kabzatul Kharij** <note>Arabic: *Qabd al-Kharij*, meaning "Outward Gain" or "Taking Out"</note>:—Of the foreign or non-Vedic caste <term>Mlechha</term>, unjust, a slanderer, small nose, brownish eyes, harsh voice, long nose <note>The text repeats "nose" with different descriptors</note>, black and yellow complexion, long teeth, long neck, eats spicy food. Resides in despicable places, has long mustaches, is of medium height, has a stout belly, and collects iron and stones.

4. ☰ This is named **Jamaat** <note>Arabic: *Jama'ah*, meaning "The Congregation" or "Gathering"</note>:—Of the laborer caste <term>Shudra</term>, red complexion, a painter or artist, of medium height, virtuous, fond of violence <note>likely implying a fierce or competitive nature</note>, a physician, black eyes, large mouth, spends gold freely, clever in advocacy or legal matters, large teeth, eats sweet food. Resides in schools <term>Pathshala</term>, and collects the five precious gems.

5. $\frac{\circ \circ}{\circ \circ}$ This is named **Farha** <note>Arabic: *Farah*, meaning "Joy" or "Gladness"</note>:—A writer or scribe, large body, fair complexion, humorous, clever in singing, beautiful, thin eyebrows, curly hair, deer-like eyes, thin lips. Resides near water, eats sweet food, has a wide mouth, and collects pearls and silver.

6. $\frac{\circ \circ}{\circ \circ}$ This is named **Ukula** <note>Arabic: *Uqlah*, meaning "The Bound" or "The Threshold"</note>:—Of low caste, black complexion, medium roundness of face, short stature, soiled or unclean, small nose, hooded eyes like a cat, troubled or sorrowful, long hair, clever, small head. Resides in prisons, caves, or dark places; a slanderer, large lips, large teeth, short neck, broad chest, long talons or fingers, and collects lead and black stone.

7. ☰ This is named **Ankish** <note>Arabic: *Ankis*, meaning "The Inverted" or "Conjoined"</note>:—A servant or slave. Black, tall, clever in agricultural work, black eyes that resemble a cat's, dressed in poor clothing, clever in worldly affairs, foul mouth, hard teeth and nails, eats very little, lazy, eats spicy food, a liar, small but elongated head, harsh voice, and collects iron and black stone.

8. $\frac{\circ}{\text{—}}$ This is named **Hamra** <note>Arabic: *Humrah*, meaning "Redness"</note>:—Of the Warrior caste <term>Kshatriya</term>, brave, a surgeon <note>literally "one who uses instruments"</note>, a thief, fond of violence, a slanderer, a blacksmith, skilled in the art of war, tawny eyes, marks or scars on the face, large head, medium height, fond of spicy things. Resides in forests, mountains, or caves, and collects diamonds <term>Vajra</term>.

9. <gloss>$\frac{॥}{—}$</gloss> <note>This symbol represents the figure 'Al-Bayad' (The White).</note> The name of this is **Bayad.**—Caste: Brahmin <note>The priestly or intellectual class</note>, fair complexion, fast gait, happy disposition, devoted to the worship of deities and religious duties. Medium height, round face, darkish eyes, sweet-spoken. Fond of fragrances like sandalwood and camphor. A seller of pearls, residing in marshy areas or near water and trees. Fond of high-quality clothing and sweet food. A collector of crystals and beads.

10. <gloss>$\frac{०}{\stackrel{०}{—}}$</gloss> <note>This symbol represents 'Nusrat al-Kharij' (Outward Victory).</note> The name of this is **Nusrutul Kharij**:—Caste: Kshatriya <note>The warrior or ruling class</note>, expert in statecraft, religious. Medium height, fair complexion, small nose, large eyes, round face, small head, slender neck. Resides near water. Wears gold and high-quality garments. Black hair, love for sweet food. A collector of gold, rubies, and precious gems.

11. <gloss>$\frac{॥}{—}$</gloss> <note>This symbol represents 'Nusrat al-Dakhil' (Inward Victory).</note> The name of this is **Nusrutul Dakhil**:—Caste: Brahmin, fair complexion, ascetic, learned and tall. Round face with mole marks, slim waist, thin calves, curly hair, large eyes. Fond of white clothes. A student and a teacher (Guru). Fond of fragrances and sweet food. A collector of gold, silver, and quartz crystals. Resides in temples, the homes of teachers, or palaces.

12. <gloss>$\frac{०}{\stackrel{०}{\stackrel{०}{—}}}$</gloss> <note>This symbol represents 'Utbat al-Kharij' (The Outer Threshold).</note> The name of this is **Utpatul Kharij**:—Caste: Mlechha <note>A term used for foreigners or those outside the traditional Vedic social system</note>. Tall, lean, unattractive, black and yellow complexion, small head, weak, black hair. Spots all over the body, eyes like a goat. Wears woolen clothes like blankets. Foul-smelling. Excessive hair on the body. Resides in forests or forts. A collector of stones.

13. <gloss>$\frac{०}{\stackrel{०}{—}}$</gloss> <note>This symbol represents 'Naqi al-Khad' (The Pure/The Cheek).</note> The name of this is **Naki**:—Caste: Kshatriya, fair complexion, short stature, lean with bluish eyes. Brave, round head, small mouth, heroic voice. A bearer of weapons, a leader of heroes. Sparse teeth, youthful appearance, a servant. Large lips, dependent on others, reddish hair. Fond of wine and meat, speaks with a lisp. Wears yellow clothes. A collector of brass and coral.

14. <gloss>$\frac{०}{—}$</gloss> <note>This symbol represents 'Utbat al-Dakhil' (The Inner Threshold).</note> The name of this is **Utpatul Dakhil**:—Caste: Common folk, tall body, reddish complexion, young, harsh, beautiful face. Sparse eyebrows, long thighs, darkish eyes, moles on the body. A collector of superior goods. Resides near trees or marshy places. A collector of indigo.

# The Method of Questioning Instruments

After first preparing the <term>Kundali</term><note>A square astrological chart or horoscope used in divination</note> according to the method described hereafter to answer the querent's question, one must determine whether the chart is true or false. Following this, the instruments (<term>Upakarana</term>) that provide strength to the question are described below. One should provide the answer based on these. There are 9 types of such instruments:

1. Maratib, 2. Imtijaj, 3. Tasir, 4. Takrar, 5. Inkilab, 6. Balabal, 7. Drishtaphala, 8. Prashnabheda, and 9. Ramal-Jivha.

## The Method of the Maratib Instrument

There are 5 divisions within this instrument, and their names are: 1. Ruvai, 2. Samani, 3. Savai, 4. Khumasi, and 5. Sudasi.

## 2. The Method of the Imtijaj Apparatus.

The third figure produced by the multiplication of two figures is given the name <term>Imtijaj</term> <note>Arabic term for "combination" or "mixture"; in geomancy, this refers to the synthesis of two figures to find a hidden outcome</note>.

If that *Imtijaj* figure is produced by multiplying two auspicious figures and the resulting third figure is also auspicious, then whatever the question regarding the task or house may be, it will grant immediate happiness and success from beginning to end.

If that figure is produced by multiplying an auspicious and an inauspicious figure, and the third figure comes out auspicious, there will be happiness at the beginning but sorrow at the end, and the successful result will be delayed.

If that figure is produced by multiplying an inauspicious and an auspicious figure, or two inauspicious figures, and the third figure comes out auspicious, there will be sorrow at the beginning, but a happy result will be obtained at the very end after a long delay.

If two inauspicious figures are multiplied and the third figure is inauspicious, only a small portion of the intended task will be accomplished.

If an auspicious and an inauspicious figure are multiplied and the third figure is inauspicious, a mixed result will be obtained.

If two inauspicious figures are multiplied and the third is also inauspicious, it results in total loss.

## The Method of the Tasir Apparatus.

After preparing the chart <note>original: "kundali"</note>, the 1st house should be understood as the querent <note>the person asking the question</note>; consider this the Ascendant or the Rising Sign. Following that house, the remaining 11 houses relate to the querent's affairs. Astrologers in Arab countries and other regions consider the remaining 13th, 14th, and 15th...

<summary>This page explains the "Imtijaj" method of combining geomantic figures to predict outcomes and begins describing the "Tasir" method for interpreting astrological houses. It provides specific rules for determining the success of a query based on whether the resulting figures are auspicious or inauspicious.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of astrological houses and their relationships, specifically addressing complex queries and the concept of repeating figures.</meta>

<page-num>47</page-num>

These four positions (13 through 16) are also used for calculations. Even when these positions are used, each one maintains a relationship with three specific houses from the primary twelve. For example: positions 1, 5, and 9 in the <term>Kundali</term><note>An astrological chart or birth map</note> are related to the 13th position. Positions 2, 6, and 10 relate to the 14th; 3, 7, and 11 relate to the 15th; and 4, 8, and 12 relate to the 16th. If it is deemed necessary to consider even more complex house relationships, one should rotate the chart starting again from the 1st house to identify the connections. 

For example: suppose someone asks a question such as, "I wish to take ancestral wealth from my brother through deception and give it to my son; however, because my wife is afflicted by a spirit <note>original: "bhutabadha" - refers to possession or supernatural illness</note> and living with her has become difficult, I want to go to Pune, earn thousands of rupees, spend them all as I please, meet my paternal uncle, and spend my time protecting my mother who is currently with my grandson." 

In this case, "I" represents the 1st house. The "brother's" house is the 3rd; the "ancestral wealth" near him is the 4th house; "deception" is the 5th house; the "son's" house is also the 5th; the "wife's" house is the 7th; the "affliction" <note>illness or obstacles</note> is the 6th house; "going to Pune" <note>long-distance travel</note> is the 9th house; "earning rupees" relates to the 2nd and 11th houses; "spending/wasting" is the 12th house; the "paternal uncle" is the 6th house; the "meeting" is the 8th house; the "grandson and mother" are the 10th house; and "protecting/preserving" is the 1st house. 

By understanding the relationship of all houses starting from the 1st, and based on the auspicious or inauspicious results of the <term>Shakals</term><note>Geomantic figures or symbols formed by dots</note> present in those houses—along with other tools or following the methods described in Part 2—one should provide the answer. The above example pertains to the querent themselves. However, if the question is, "My brother is going to do these things," then one must imagine the 3rd house (the brother's house) as the 1st house or <term>Lagna</term><note>The Ascendant or starting point</note> and rotate the chart's house relationships accordingly. By doing this, no room for doubt will remain.

## The Method of the Repeating Tool (Takrar)

If a <term>Shakal</term> <note>geomantic figure</note> that has fallen in any one house of the chart appears again in any of the remaining 15 houses, that repeating figure is called <term>Takrar</term> <note>literally "complaint" or "repetition"; here meaning a recurring geomantic sign</note> or "the repeated." There are eight types of such repetitions.

**Repetition 1:—If the figure <term>Shakal</term><note>A geomantic figure or symbol formed by points</note> that first appears is auspicious and falls in an auspicious house <term>Sthana</term><note>One of the twelve astrological houses or positions in a chart</note>, and then repeats <term>Takrar</term><note>Literally 'dispute' or 'repetition'; refers to the same figure appearing in multiple houses</note> in other auspicious houses, it yields the most excellent results.**

**Repetition 2:—If that figure is auspicious but falls in an inauspicious house and repeats in an auspicious house; or, if it is auspicious and falls in an auspicious house but repeats in an inauspicious house, it yields good results.**

**Repetition 3:—If that figure is auspicious but falls in an inauspicious house and repeats in an inauspicious house, it yields middling results.**

**Repetition 4:—If that figure is inauspicious and falls in an inauspicious house and repeats in an inauspicious house, it yields very poor or inferior results.**

**Repetition 5:—If that figure is inauspicious and falls in an inauspicious house but repeats in an auspicious house; or, if it is inauspicious and falls in an auspicious house but repeats in an inauspicious house, it yields poor results.**

**Repetition 6:—If that figure is inauspicious but falls in an auspicious house and repeats in an auspicious house, it yields (half) middling-poor results.**

**Repetition 7:—The six methods described above explain how to predict outcomes based on the repetition of figures in just two houses. However, depending on the seeker's <term>Karma</term><note>Actions or destiny</note>, repeating figures often appear in more than two houses in a divination chart <term>Prashna-Kundali</term>. Whether they fall in auspicious, inauspicious, or a mix of both types of houses, one must judge the strength of the result by weighing the auspicious or inauspicious nature of those specific houses as explained above.**

**Repetition 8:—The previous seven methods showed the relationship between auspicious and inauspicious figures. However, among the sixteen figures, two are inherently "middling" in their results. To predict the outcome of their repetition, one must keep all the above rules in mind and declare the result based on the auspicious or inauspicious nature of the houses in which they appear.**

<summary>This page outlines eight rules for interpreting the repetition of geomantic figures across different houses, categorizing the outcomes from "most excellent" to "very poor" based on the harmony between the figure's nature and the house's quality. It emphasizes that the final prediction must be adjusted based on the specific houses occupied in a divination chart.</summary>

<keywords>geomancy, Takrar, repetition, Shakal, Sthana, auspicious, inauspicious, divination chart, Prashna-Kundali, interpretation rules</keywords>

## The Method of the Inkilab Instrument.

Once the primary divination chart <note>Prashna Kundali: a horary chart used to answer a specific question</note> is prepared, multiply the figures in houses 1, 2, 3, and 4 by the figures in houses 5, 6, 7, and 8 respectively—that is, multiply the first by the fifth, the second by the sixth, the third by the seventh, and the fourth by the eighth. From these four resulting figures, construct a separate complete chart. In the 15th house of this new chart, the figure ☰ <term>Jama'at</term> <note>original: "जमात" (Arabic: al-Jama'a); represents a gathering or congregation</note> will undoubtedly appear. This is derived by multiplying the figures in the 13th and 14th houses.

If that <term>Jama'at</term> figure is produced from two auspicious <term>Dakhil</term> <note>Entering/Incoming</note> figures, then a favorable result is obtained for matters involving arrivals or gains. If produced from inauspicious <term>Dakhil</term> figures, the result for such matters is unfavorable. If produced from auspicious <term>Kharij</term> <note>Outgoing/Leaving</note> figures, a favorable result is obtained for matters involving departures or exits. If from inauspicious <term>Kharij</term> figures, the result for departures is unfavorable. If produced from auspicious <term>Sabit</term> <note>Stable/Fixed</note> figures, a favorable result for stable or long-term matters is obtained. If from inauspicious <term>Sabit</term> figures, the result for stable matters is unfavorable. If produced from auspicious <term>Munqalib</term> <note>Movable/Changing</note> figures, a favorable result for neutral or changing matters is obtained; if from inauspicious <term>Munqalib</term> figures, the result is unfavorable. This Inkilab instrument should be used for all inquiries except for "fist-questions" <note>guessing an object hidden in a hand</note>, silent questions <note>where the querent does not speak the question aloud</note>, yearly forecasts, time-limit determinations, and identifying a thief.

## The Method of the Balabal Instrument.

Whichever figures in the chart fall in their "own houses" <note>natural or assigned positions</note> are considered powerful for the affairs of those houses. If the same figure appears two or more times according to the repetition rules, it becomes even more powerful. If they are not in their own houses, they should be considered weak.

## The Method of the Drishtibal Instrument.

There are 5 divisions of "aspects" <note>Drishti: the way figures 'look' at or influence one another based on their positions</note>; their names are: 1st <term>Tarbiya</term> <note>Square aspect (90°)</note>; 2nd <term>Tasdis</term> <note>Sextile aspect (60°)</note>; 3rd <term>Taslis</term> <note>Trine aspect (120°)</note>; 4th <term>Muqabila</term> <note>Opposition (180°)</note>; and 5th <term>Muqarna</term> <note>Conjunction (0°)</note>.

---

<note>The figure that appears in the 15th house of the primary chart is the exact same figure that invariably appears in the 1st and 14th houses of the Inkilab chart. Given this, it is unclear why the original researchers wrote a method in the texts to prepare an entirely separate Inkilab chart. Readers should investigate the reason for this.</note>

**The 1st Aspect: Square <term>Tarbiya-drishti; an aspect of 90 degrees</term>:-** The 1st house represents the position of the querent. The figure located in the 3rd house looks upon this 1st house. It gives results—whether auspicious or inauspicious—accordingly <note>The text suggests a specific numerical strength or influence of 4 units here</note>.

**The 2nd Aspect: Sextile <term>Tasdi-drishti; an aspect of 60 degrees</term>:-** The figure in the 5th house looks upon the 1st house. It gives eight units of result, whether auspicious or inauspicious.

**The 3rd Aspect: Trine <term>Nasalli-drishti; an aspect of 120 degrees</term>:-** The figure in the 4th house looks upon the 1st house. It gives twelve units of result, whether auspicious or inauspicious.

**The 4th Aspect: Opposition <term>Muqabila-drishti; an aspect of 180 degrees</term>:-** The figure in the 7th house looks upon the 1st house. It gives full results, whether auspicious or inauspicious, as the case may be.

**The 5th Aspect: Conjunction <term>Muqarna-drishti; an aspect of 0 degrees or proximity</term>:-** The figure in the 12th house looks upon the 1st house. It gives "mute" results, whether auspicious or inauspicious; that is to say, its contribution is not clearly understood.

In this manner, for whichever houses are related to the query, one should examine the aforementioned aspect results in both clockwise and counter-clockwise directions.

In these aspects, there are two types: **Hidden** and **Manifest**.

**Hidden Aspect <term>Gupta-drishti</term>:-** When a figure sits in its own natural home according to the geomantic sequence and looks upon the house of the query, it is called a Hidden Aspect. This is considered more powerful.

**Manifest Aspect <term>Prakat-drishti</term>:-** When a figure is not in its own natural home but looks upon the house of the query, it is called a Manifest Aspect. Although its strength is less, it is still capable of giving results. For example, a chart has been prepared. The querent's question is about "Fate" <term>Daiva-vichara</term>. In that case, the 1st house represents Fate. Suppose the figure **U** <note>original: ठं - likely representing a specific geomantic sign like 'Acquisitio' or 'Laetitia' in this system</note> falls in that house. To see which full aspect from the 7th house affects it, if that house contains its own natural figure according to the sequence, then the aspect is Hidden and should be known as more powerful. However, if the figure **N** <note>original: नूं</note> is in that house, it should be known as a Manifest Aspect and not in its own home.

**Method for Dakhil Questions:**—When the question is of the Dakhil type (concerning the acquisition of all kinds of tasks/works) and Dakhil figures appear in the 1st, 14th, and 15th houses of the Kundali <term>Kundali: the geomantic chart or square</term>, if they are auspicious, the task will be completed quickly and without effort. If they are inauspicious, the task will be completed with delay. If Kharij figures appear in those houses and are auspicious, the effort made for that task will go in vain. If they are inauspicious, the task will not happen at all. If Sabit figures appear in those houses and are auspicious, the task is completed with delay. If they are inauspicious, the task will not happen. If they are mediocre, there will be mediocre success. And if Munkalib figures appear in all three of those houses, whether they are auspicious or inauspicious, the task will not be accomplished.

**Method for Kharij Questions:**—When the question is of the Kharij type (concerning the departure or loss of all kinds of tasks) and if auspicious or inauspicious Dakhil figures appear in the 1st, 14th, and 15th houses of the chart, the task will not be accomplished no matter how much effort is made. If auspicious or inauspicious Sabit figures appear in those houses, the task does not happen. If Munkalib figures are present and are auspicious, the task will be fully accomplished. If they are inauspicious, the task will be accomplished through laziness <note>likely implying a slow or sluggish process</note>. If Kharij figures in those houses are auspicious, the work will undoubtedly be done. If they are inauspicious, it will be done through great effort.

**Method for Sabit Questions:**—When the question is of the Sabit type (concerning the stability of all kinds of tasks) and if auspicious Sabit or auspicious Dakhil figures appear in the 1st, 14th, and 15th houses...

If the figures are auspicious, the work will be accomplished with ease. If inauspicious, the work will be achieved through great hardship. **The Method for Mutable Questions:** The sequence mentioned above in the method for *Kharij* questions applies to this method as well, hence it is not discussed separately. *Dakhol* <note>Incoming</note> and *Sabit* <note>Stable</note> figures mostly yield the same results, while *Kharij* and *Munkalib* figures yield results of a similar nature.

**Method when Contradictory Figures Appear:** If the figures in houses 1, 14, and 15 of the horoscope <note>original: "Kundali" - the geomantic chart</note> do not fall according to the four methods mentioned above but are instead contradictory to one another, then the figures in those three houses should be multiplied together to create a single figure. One should then observe whether that figure is *Dakhol*, *Kharij*, *Sabit*, or *Munkalib*, and whether it is auspicious or inauspicious, and provide the answer based on which of the four methods it fits. For example: If in houses 1, 14, and 15 of the chart, the figures <term>°°/°°</term> <note>The figure of 'Populus' or People</note>, <term>°/°°</term> <note>The figure of 'Albus' or White</note>, and <term>°°/°</term> <note>The figure of 'Puella' or Girl</note> appear—representing *Kharij*, *Dakhol*, and *Sabit* respectively—they are contradictory. As per the method, multiplying the figure in the 1st house <term>°°/°°</term> with the 14th house <term>°/°°</term> results in the figure <term>°/°°</term>. Then, multiplying this resulting figure by the 15th house figure <term>°°/°</term> produces <term>°/°</term> <note>The figure of 'Amissio' or Loss</note>, which is inauspicious and a *Munkalib* figure. Based on this, one should provide the answer by considering the nature of the task as explained in the 4th method. The method of multiplication and the method of drawing the chart have been written previously.

**The Method of the Ramal-Jivha Tool:** In this tool <note>original: "Upakarana" - instrument or apparatus</note>, there are 11 sequences: 1. Omen (*Shakun*), 2. A.B.D.H., 3. Bi. J. D. H., 4. An. B. J. D., 5. Temperament (*Mizaj*), 6. Literal/Alphabetic (*Harfi*), 7. Essence (*Assah*), 8. Decree (*Hukum*), 9. Petition (*Arj*), 10. Return (*Ma'ad*), and 11. Triangle (*Musallas*).

**Omen Sequence:** This sequence should be used for all types of questions.

**Abdah Sequence:** This should be used to determine a thief's appearance, qualities, number of offspring, and to decide the specific day.

**A. B. J. D. Sequence:** This should be used for identifying the names of objects, the origin of numbers <note>original: "Ankotpatti"</note>, and for the examination of water.

# The Abda-hadi System of Numerical Analysis.
<note>The "Abda-hadi" (A-B-D-H) system refers to a specific method of assigning numerical values to the four levels of a geomantic figure, likely derived from Arabic "Abjad" numerology.</note>

The method of the A. B. D. H. row is given as an example. The number for 'A' is 1; for 'B' is 2; for 'D' is 4; and for 'H' is 8. Accordingly, fixed numbers are assigned to those specific letters. Except for the 4th and 16th <term>Shakal</term><note>A 'Shakal' is one of the sixteen geomantic figures or signs used in divination.</note>, all other figures contain both dots and lines. The 4th contains only lines, and the 16th contains only dots. From the top to the bottom of each figure, the lines and dots inherently represent the four <term>elements</term><note>Tattvas</note> in this order: **Fire, Air, Water, and Earth**. In these figures, all dots are considered "manifest" elements, and all lines are considered "hidden" elements. When calculating the total sum, one must take the numbers assigned to the manifest elements (dots) and add them together. The 16th figure <insert>०<br/>०<br/>०<br/>०</insert> <note>This figure is known as 'Laetitia' or 'Joy' in Western geomancy, consisting of four dots.</note> consists of four dots. Its sequential numbers are 1-2-4-8. Adding these numbers results in the sum of 15. Therefore, it is placed in the 15th position. In the 15th figure <insert>—<br/>०<br/>०<br/>—</insert>, the positions for Fire and Earth are "hidden" elements (lines); therefore, excluding them and adding the numbers for the Air and Water elements (2 and 4) results in 6. Based on this, the figure <insert>—<br/>०<br/>०<br/>—</insert> is placed in the 6th position. This is the method of the A. B. D. H. sequence. For example, if a question regarding the number of children arises, following the method described in the later section on questioning, if this figure <insert>०<br/>०<br/>—<br/>०</insert> is produced: by excluding the single line (hidden element) and adding the remaining numbers 1, 2, and 8, the sum is 11. From this, one should tell the querent that they will have 11 children. Similarly, calculations should be made using the sums of the sequences Bi. 2, Ja. 7, Da. 4, Ha. 8 and A. 1, Ba. 2, Ja. 3, Da. 4. In some places, a method of doubling the numbers for lines while keeping the numbers for zeros (dots) constant is described further on.

## Determining Strength and Weakness through the Elements.

There is friendship between the elements of Fire and Air; there is friendship between Earth and Water. Likewise, there is enmity between Water and Fire; there is enmity between Earth and Air. There is moderate friendship between Fire and Earth, and moderate friendship between Water and Air.

(56)

Whatever figure belongs to the Fire element is considered strong when it resides in the "house" of the Fire element. Even if it is in a "friend's house," it should be known as strong. A figure situated in an "enemy's house" is weak, and a figure in a "neutral house" should be considered of medium strength. These elements reside within the sixteen figures, and thus they are described in their elemental forms. In this same manner, one should understand the enmities and friendships of the figures. Whichever figures belong to specific elements, they should be considered powerful in those corresponding positions. 

For example: <term>Layan</term> <note>The geomantic figure 'Laian' or 'Fortuna Minor', representing lesser fortune</note> <note>geomantic symbol</note> is itself of the Fire element. In the <term>Kundali</term> <note>The astrological or geomantic square chart</note>, the positions for the Fire element are 1, 5, 9, and 13. Therefore, if the <term>Layan</term> <note>geomantic symbol</note> figure falls in these positions, it is powerful. Now, the element of the <term>Layan</term> figure is Fire, and Fire has a friendship with the Air element. In the chart, the positions for the Air element are 2, 6, 10, and 14. If the <term>Layan</term> figure falls in these positions, it should be understood as strong.

If any figure is hidden in an enemy's house, it should be considered weak. For instance, the <term>Layan</term> <note>geomantic symbol</note> figure is of the Fire element, and the enemy of the Fire element is the Water element. The positions for the Water element in the chart are 3, 7, 11, and 15. If the <term>Layan</term> figure falls in these positions, it should be considered weak. In the same way, if any figure falls in a position of "medium friendship" <note>neutrality</note>, that figure should be known as having medium strength. For example, the <term>Layan</term> figure is of the Fire element, and its medium friend is the Earth element. The positions for the Earth element in the chart are 4, 8, 12, and 16. Therefore, if the <term>Layan</term> figure is in these positions, it should be known as having medium strength. In this manner, a practitioner of <term>Jyotish</term> <note>Astrology/Divination</note> should contemplate the figures very carefully.

# Questions for the Astrologer to Consider Privately.

The <term>Astrologer</term> <note>Marathi: Jyotishi; a practitioner of divination</note> should rise early in the morning, complete their daily religious duties such as bathing and prayers according to the faith, remember their Guru, and recite the previously mentioned mantras. Then, contemplating the question, "**How many people will come to consult me today?**" they should prepare a <term>Horoscope</term> <note>Marathi: Kundali; here referring to a Ramala geomantic square or chart</note>:—

**Method 1:**—In that <term>Horoscope</term>, from houses 1 to 16, observe which <term>Figures</term> <note>Marathi: Shakla; the sixteen geomantic signs</note> have fallen in accordance with the <term>Bi. Ja. Da. Ha.</term> <note>A mnemonic for the four elements: Badi (Air), Jal (Water), Dar (Earth), and Har (Fire)</note> rows mentioned in the <term>Ramala-Jivha</term> <note>The "Tongue of Ramala," a specific technical manual or instrument for this divination</note> table. People will arrive in numbers corresponding to the <term>Bi. Ja. Da. Ha.</term> values of those figures. If figures of those specific numbers do not appear, no one will come.

**Method 2:**—Multiply the <term>Figures</term> in houses 1 and 13 together to produce a single <term>Figure</term>. Observe how many times that <term>Figure</term> repeats <note>Marathi: Takrar; the repetition of a geomantic sign in different houses</note> within the <term>Horoscope</term>, and examine the auspicious or inauspicious aspects cast upon those repeating <term>Figures</term>. One should understand that the number of people arriving will match the <term>Bi. Ja. Da. Ha.</term> count of the figures receiving an auspicious aspect.

## What will they come to ask?

The <term>Figure</term> resulting from the multiplication of the figures in houses 1 and 13 will repeat in certain houses of the <term>Horoscope</term>; the clients will ask questions related to the significations of those specific houses.

## What is the nature of the questioners?

If the <term>Figure</term> resulting from the multiplication of houses 7 and 9 is inauspicious and repeats in an inauspicious house, then the questioners have come to mock or slander the astrologer. This method can be used at any time.

## Will the questioners bring any offerings?

Multiply the <term>Figures</term> in the four houses 1, 13, 11, and 14 with each other to produce one final <term>Figure</term>. If that resulting <term>Figure</term> is already present elsewhere in the <term>Horoscope</term>, they will bring something. Alternatively, if it is a <term>Figure</term> of the <term>Air</term> or <term>Fire element</term>, they will also bring something. If the figures belong to the remaining elements, they will bring nothing.

## What will they bring?

In the <term>Figure</term> resulting from the multiplication of houses 1, 13, 11, and 14: if the <term>Fire element point</term> is prominent, they bring wealth; if the <term>Air element point</term> is prominent, they bring a living being; if the <term>Water point</term> is prominent, they bring fruit; and if the <term>Earth point</term> is prominent, they bring a root-based substance <note>Likely referring to grains, tubers, or solid materials</note>.

### Method for Understanding the Thoughts of the Mind

The figure resulting from multiplying the figures in positions 1 and 13 will indicate the nature of the inquiry based on which houses it "complains" to <note>takrar: a technical term likely referring to the aspect or relationship between houses in the chart</note> in the chart. If that figure does not "complain" and is not present in the chart at all, then it should be understood that the question does not belong to the querent.

**Method 2:**—Excluding the non-indicator (-) points* from all 16 positions of the chart, count only the indicator (०) points and divide that total by 16. Based on the remainder that is left, one should judge that the question pertains to that specific house.

**Example:**—The total count of only the points in all sixteen positions is 52. Dividing that number by 16 leaves a remainder of 4. From this, one should understand that the question pertains to the 4th house of the chart.

**Method 3:**—Create one figure by taking the Earth-element lines and points from the four positions 15, 13, 9, and 1. Create one figure by taking the Fire-element lines and points from positions 1, 2, 3, and 4. Create one figure by taking the Water-element lines and points from positions 5, 6, 7, and 8. Create a half-figure by taking the Air-element lines and points from the two positions 8 and 12.

### The Method of Moving the Points

The upper point present in the 15th house of the chart is revealed by a certain element <note>original: "tattva"</note>; it is situated in the figure of the 13th or 14th house in the place of that same element. By taking that point upward from there, it goes and sits in the place of the same revealed element in any one of the figures in the 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th houses. If moved further in the same sequence, it settles in a figure within any two houses from 1 to 8. In the same manner, the lower point should be moved upward according to whichever element it belongs to; it also settles in one figure among the first 8 houses, or both points may settle in the same figure. One point may ascend through the right half of the chart and the other through the left half, or both may ascend through the same part in the same figure. There is no reason to doubt this.

### Results of the Position of Points or Figures.

If a point of the **Fire element** is positioned within a **Fire figure**, it indicates concerns regarding a house, a temple, the acquisition of wealth, or other auspicious works.

If a point of the **Fire element** is positioned within **Air figures**, it indicates concerns regarding profit, bodily health, auspicious works, and so on.

If a point of the **Fire element** is positioned within a **Water figure**, it indicates concerns regarding coming and going <note>travel or transitions</note>, marriage, partnerships, and so on.

If a point of the **Fire element** is positioned within an **Earth figure**, it indicates thoughts regarding disease, life, and paternal property, and so on.

If an **Air point** is positioned within a **Fire figure**, it indicates friendship, the acquisition of wealth, and so on.

If an **Air point** is positioned within an **Air figure**, it indicates concerns regarding disease, hidden treasures, and so on.

If an **Air point** is positioned within a **Water figure**, it indicates thoughts regarding travel, education, friendship, and so on.

If an **Air point** is positioned within an **Earth figure**, it indicates thoughts regarding enemies and friends, and so on.

If a **Water point** is positioned within a **Fire figure**, it indicates travel and the commencement of work, and so on.

If a **Water point** is positioned within an **Air figure**, it indicates wealth, disease, news of someone fleeing, the sending of goods, and so on.

If a **Water point** is positioned within a **Water figure**, it indicates marriage, sensual desires, and so on.

If a **Water point** is positioned within an **Earth figure**, it indicates foreign travel, thoughts regarding servants, and so on.

If an **Earth point** is positioned within a **Fire figure**, it indicates the acquisition of land, hope for wealth, thoughts of enmity, and so on.

> In the case of a silent question, one should not perform the work at all. If one does so through negligence, then they are excluded from the path of righteousness. || 18 || Therefore, the God of Gods, the Supreme Lord, knows all; I am nothing, but I speak a little according to the rules of the scriptures. || 19 || <note>original Sanskrit: "मूकप्रश्ने प्रतिज्ञावें... प्रवदाम्यहं"</note>

**Meaning:—** Matters such as the anxieties of the mind, secret affairs, the name of a thief or any specific person, or going to a place where treasure is buried—such tasks should not be told by the <term>Astrologer</term> <note>Marathi: Jyotishikya; here referring to the geomancer</note>. One should not go to such places. Even if the questioner asks out of ignorance or error, one should ignore their inquiry and wait until at least a small essence of the question comes from the questioner's mouth; only then should the <term>Astrologer</term> describe it according to their intellect. Regarding this, it is written in both Sanskrit and Yavana <note>Greek or Perso-Arabic</note> texts that it is improper for humans to interfere in the workings of the Lord who moves the world; therefore, one should act after considering the country, time, and circumstances.

### Determination of Time

At the time when the question horoscope is to be prepared, divide that time into four parts. Based on the <term>Umahat</term> <note>Arabic: 'Ummahat' meaning 'The Mothers', the first four figures in a geomantic chart</note> row in the horoscope, determine the accidental or sudden time. Based on the forefront of the <term>Umahat</term> row—that is, the 'handless' row—determine the past. Based on the forefront of the previously mentioned row—that is, the <term>Muttabalidaat</term> <note>likely a corruption of 'Muttalidaat', the 'Generated' figures or Daughters</note> row—determine the present time. Below that row, based on the 'own house' or property, determine the future time. In this way, the decision of time should be made. In whichever house a favorable <term>Shakal</term> <note>Arabic: 'Shakl', meaning a geomantic figure or sign</note> resides, the success of the task will occur during the time associated with that <term>Shakal</term>.

**Method 2:—** Multiply the <term>Shakal</term> in the 1st house by the <term>Shakal</term> in the 4th house; the resulting <term>Shakal</term> indicates the past. Multiply the <term>Shakal</term> in the 7th house by the <term>Shakal</term> in the 10th house; the resulting <term>Shakal</term> indicates the future. Know that the <term>Shakal</term> resulting from multiplying the upper figure by the lower figure indicates the present time.

**Method 3:—** Houses 1-5-9-13 show the present time. Houses 2-6-10-14 show the future time. Houses 3-7-11-15 show the past time, and houses 4-8-12-16 show the accidental or sudden time.

**Method 4:—** Houses 1-2-3-4 indicate <term>Ghatikas</term> <note>a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> and days. Houses 5-6-7-8 indicate days and weeks. Houses 9-10-11-12 indicate weeks and months. Houses 13-14-15-16 indicate months and years.
